Midway through this article I got the distinct feeling I was reading an undergraduate essay -- albeit a decently researched one. Sure enough the author Melody Guan is about to graduate from Harvard and is into writing pieces covering the "tech scene" for Harvard and Huffpost. It's admirable, but this piece isn't much besides a rehash of recent quotes by other notables.

Some of her assertions are flat out unsupported, and some of the positions taken by the economists she quotes are far from accepted. For example it is the notable LACK of productivity gains in the past decade that has economists puzzled, despite the perpetual march of technology -- the hollowing out of the middle class would not be happening if productivity were rising. If technology adoption and automation drove productivity as asserted, we would be seeing strong growth everywhere in the US, not scrawny 2% GDP numbers. In fact, Hal Varian (economist now with Google) posits that what's actually broken are economist's methods of measuring productivity and quality-of-life. It might be far better than we are reporting. Or it might not. Perhaps for a digitized future, our agro-industrial economic measures are coming up short in so many areas, policy needs to be rewritten and rethought.

Furthermore, this article conflates robotics with the development of advanced General AI "artillect" -- these are hugely different topics. Robotics is largely a hardware, engineering, sensor, and even a "wetware" type of problem. Ben Goertzel argues compellingly that software emulation on virtual agents is the ideal platform to develop artificial general intelligence, anyway, and it seems utterly logical to me. It isn't as though I don't expect great strides in robotics, but to me robotics are a sideshow to the development of AI. We will have a thinking neuro-chip before we have a useful and affordable bipedal robot.

As for job losses, meh. I am completely unconvinced that anything but a temporarily-high unemployment is in the cards. We saw it in the transition from agricultural to industrial society and we will see it again. Heck we might even be living in the early transition period right now, which would explain some things. *Persistently" high unemployment is more indicative of bad economic policy, inflation, bad governance, and other more mundane problems that have no bearing on technology. The creative destruction that obliterated farming as an occupation has simultaneously created an abundance of food and obesity epidemics. The destruction of unneeded workers frees those workers up to do things elsewhere. My ancestors were farmers and industrial workers, however my wife and I make essentially nothing physical -- just collected digital ones and zeroes that some other humans find valuable. I think people will keep finding value with and between each other in the future, so there is no real need to worry about that.

All of the proposed legislation that I have heard in the past 10 years would not have stopped this shooting.

Mandatory waiting period: The shooter waited almost two months from when he ordered his handgun to when he actually used it to kill, which is longer than every state mandated waiting period that I know.

Mandatory background checks: He bought it from a store, which means he had a background check. The criteria for passing a background check are sound- no felonies, outstanding warrants, DUI, restraining orders, history of mental illness... plus some other obscure ones.

Gun registry: Irrelevant. If he planned on killing himself after (which almost all 'mass' shooters do) he doesn't care if they can trace the gun back to him.

Assault rifle ban: Irrelevant. Rifles are used in less than 3% of the gun deaths in the US... and this dude used a handgun.
